{"id": "ee413dd5-10da-45d8-8086-a8bdcbf1cc96", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_3JBjea5DSq3BvkiukMXaJv", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"---\\\\r\\\\nname: aws-routing\\\\r\\\\ndescription: \\'Use this skill when the user wants to know which path AWS will pick for their traffic, why traffic took an unexpected route, or how to make AWS prefer a path. Covers Cloud WAN CNE route evaluation, Direct Connect Gateway local vs remote region preference, Transit Gateway route tables, ECMP and peering, VPC longest-prefix-match, BGP traffic engineering (LP communities 7224:7100/7200/7300, AS-path prepending, MED), DX + VPN redundancy and failover, and asymmetric routing. Use it even when the user only describes a symptom, such as \\\\\"traffic is leaving the region\\\\\", \\\\\"not using my local Direct Connect\\\\\", \\\\\"routing to the wrong VIF/location\\\\\", or \\\\\"path is asymmetric\\\\\". Read-only: analysis, recommendations, and describe/get/list validation commands grounded in public AWS docs.\\'\\\\r\\\\nmetadata:\\\\r\\\\n  version: \\\\\"1.2.6\\\\\"\\\\r\\\\n  summary: \\\\\"Explains which path AWS picks across Cloud WAN, Transit Gateway, Direct Connect and VPN, why traffic took an unexpected route, and how to steer it.\\\\\"\\\\r\\\\n  author: midakin\\\\r\\\\n  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: \\\\\"CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA\\\\\"\\\\r\\\\n---\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n## Overview\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\nThis skill provides routing-first analysis for AWS networking. If you lack a verified\\\\r\\\\n  source, state \\\\\"I cannot verify this\\\\\" rather than inventing details.\\\\r\\\\n- State assumptions explicitly before answering.\\\\r\\\\n- Cross-check each claim against public AWS documentation or the `references/` files. Establish the path.** Identify source, destination, and every routing construct in\\\\r\\\\n  between (VPC route table \\\\u2192 TGW/Cloud WAN CNE \\\\u2192 DXGW \\\\u2192 VIF \\\\u2192 on-prem, or the relevant subset).\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **2. Name the route table.** Be explicit about which table makes each decision (VPC RT, TGW RT,\\\\r\\\\n  CNE RT, DXGW internal selection).\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **3. Apply the evaluation order for that construct** (see below).\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **4. Identify the deciding attribute** (longest prefix, local preference, AS-path, MED, source\\\\r\\\\n  type).\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **5. Flag non-determinism** (e.g., ECMP or \\\\\"deterministically random\\\\\" tiebreakers) and\\\\r\\\\n  recommend a deterministic alternative.\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **6. Cite the AWS documentation** that supports the behavior.\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **7. Provide read-only validation commands** the user can run to confirm.\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **8. Self-check before answering.** Re-read the answer against steps 1-7: every route table is\\\\r\\\\n  named, the evaluation order matches the construct, each cited URL was actually retrieved, and every\\\\r\\\\n  command is read-only. Fix any gap before presenting.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n## Key evaluation rules\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### Every route table does its own lookup\\\\r\\\\nEach construct that owns a route table makes its own decision. The DXGW is a distributed set of BGP\\\\r\\\\nroute reflectors outside the data path: it selects the best VIF per prefix and reflects it, so a TGW\\\\r\\\\nor Cloud WAN CNE sees the DXGW as (usually) a single next hop and traffic goes straight to that VIF.\\\\r\\\\nThere is no second packet lookup at the DXGW.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### ECMP is an outcome, not a step\\\\r\\\\nLongest prefix match comes first (a route lookup, not a BGP attribute). Then BGP attributes are\\\\r\\\\ncompared in order and selection stops at the first attribute that differs. If all of them are equal,\\\\r\\\\nthe result is ECMP.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### Cloud WAN (per CNE)\\\\r\\\\nLongest prefix match first; then static \\\\u2192 system routes (1:1 NAT) \\\\u2192 VPC-propagated (same region) \\\\u2192\\\\r\\\\ndynamic routes compared in order, stopping at the first difference: local preference set by a Cloud\\\\r\\\\nWAN routing policy (higher wins, default 0; its position before AS_PATH is SME-confirmed field\\\\r\\\\nknowledge) \\\\u2192 shortest AS-path \\\\u2192 lowest MED \\\\u2192 equal-attribute source preference:\\\\r\\\\nDXGW-propagated \\\\u2192 Cloud WAN Connect \\\\u2192 S2S VPN \\\\u2192 other (TGW peering, remote CNEs; identical from 2+\\\\r\\\\nsources = deterministically random, chosen per segment / network function group). With multiple\\\\r\\\\nDXGWs, Cloud WAN works differently from TGW: the CNE evaluates the route from each DXGW attachment\\\\r\\\\nitself. Steer between DXGWs with inbound Cloud WAN routing policies (`set-local-preference`,\\\\r\\\\n`prepend-asn-list`/`remove-asn-list`/`replace-asn-list`, or `set-med`; policy version 2025.11+). Without a policy, identical routes give non-deterministic selection.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### Direct Connect (private/transit VIF, outbound AWS\\\\u2192on-prem)\\\\r\\\\nLongest prefix match first; then local preference \\\\u2192 AS_PATH length \\\\u2192 MED, stopping at the first\\\\r\\\\ndifference. If all are equal, the result is ECMP across the VIFs. LP communities `7224:7300/7200/7100`\\\\r\\\\n(High/Medium/Low) set local preference and are evaluated before AS-path. These BGP attributes are\\\\r\\\\nset at the VIF level on the on-prem router\\'s advertisements and evaluated by the DXGW. DXGW prefers\\\\r\\\\nthe local associated-region DX by default. Some DX locations serve more than one Region by port\\\\r\\\\nspeed, so check the associated Region of the specific connection, not just the location.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### Transit Gateway with Direct Connect\\\\r\\\\nUse one DXGW with multiple transit VIFs for ECMP. BGP attributes stay on the VIFs and do not pass to\\\\r\\\\nthe TGW. Use multiple DXGWs only for traffic isolation or multiple primary paths. Across DXGWs on a\\\\r\\\\nTGW with no LP community and equal AS_PATH/MED, a local associated-Region DX wins on local\\\\r\\\\npreference over a remote one (no ECMP), and ECMP also needs matching DXGW Amazon-side ASNs. For\\\\r\\\\nECMP across DXGW attachments, LP communities and failover timing, load\\\\r\\\\n[Transit Gateway routing patterns](references/tgw-routing-patterns.md).\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### Direction & tooling guidance\\\\r\\\\n- **AWS \\\\u2192 on-prem (egress):** control with DX LP communities.\\\\r\\\\n- **On-prem \\\\u2192 AWS (ingress):** control with the customer router\\'s local-pref/weight/MED.\\\\r\\\\n- **AS-path prepending:** within a region only - unreliable across regions because DXGW local-region\\\\r\\\\n  LP overrides it. **LP communities:** work within-region and cross-region.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n## Reference material\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\nDetailed mechanics, patterns, and caveats are in `references/`. Load only the file that matches the\\\\r\\\\nconstruct deciding the path:\\\\r\\\\n- [Cloud WAN + DX routing patterns](references/cloudwan-dx-routing-patterns.md) - load when the path\\\\r\\\\n  crosses a Cloud WAN CNE: CNE route evaluation, DXGW path selection into Cloud WAN, community\\\\r\\\\n  traffic-engineering patterns, regional inspection, multi-region egress.\\\\r\\\\n- [Direct Connect routing patterns](references/dx-routing-patterns.md) - load when the question is\\\\r\\\\n  about a DX VIF or DXGW without Cloud WAN: BGP mechanics, BFD, MED, ASN ranges, VIF considerations,\\\\r\\\\n  CloudHub, when VIFs can talk, active/active vs active/passive.\\\\r\\\\n- [Transit Gateway routing patterns](references/tgw-routing-patterns.md) - load when VPN backs up\\\\r\\\\n  or runs alongside DX: route preference between them, ECMP limits, asymmetric return paths.\\\\r\\\\n- [Networking strategic questions](references/networking-strategic-questions.md) - load when key\\\\r\\\\n  facts are missing (regions, attachments, ASNs, communities) and you need discovery questions to ask\\\\r\\\\n  before analyzing.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n## Output expectations\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n- Explain the route-evaluation logic step by step.\\\\r\\\\n- Name the specific route table involved.\\\\r\\\\n- Give the end-to-end traffic path.\\\\r\\\\n- Compare options with tradeoffs (determinism, complexity, failover) when multiple solutions exist.\\\\r\\\\n- Include read-only AWS CLI validation commands.\\\\r\\\\n- Recommend testing in a non-production environment and blue/green for migrations.\\\\r\\\\n\", \"resource_manifest\": [\"SKILL.md\", \"references/cloudwan-dx-routing-patterns.md\", \"references/dx-routing-patterns.md\", \"references/networking-strategic-questions.md\", \"references/tgw-routing-patterns.md\", \"references/vpn-dx-redundancy-patterns.md\"]}'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "27df074d-951f-471e-9c0e-974b54f60a0f", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_MzS6y1KVBQ1gNOOyM3nTRO", "content": "[{'text': '\\r\\n\\r\\n# Transit Gateway Routing Patterns & Considerations\\r\\n\\r\\nThis document captures key routing mechanics, ECMP behavior, failover characteristics, and operational considerations for Transit Gateway architectures. Use this knowledge when advising on TGW route evaluation, multi-attachment designs, inter-region peering, and DX/VPN integration.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reference Documentation\\r\\n\\r\\n- [How transit gateways work (route evaluation order)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html)\\r\\n- [Transit Gateway quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/transit-gateway-quotas.html)\\r\\n- [Site-to-Site VPN quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-limits.html)\\r\\n- [Transit gateway peering attachments](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/tgw-peering.html)\\r\\n- [Transit Gateway FAQs](https://aws.amazon.com/transit-gateway/faqs/)\\r\\n- [Direct Connect gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-gateways-intro.html)\\r\\n- [Direct Connect routing policies and BGP communities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html)\\r\\n- [Transit Gateway VPN ECMP](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/transit-gateway-share.html)\\r\\n- [Direct Connect + Transit Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-transit-gateways.html)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Route Evaluation & Priority\\r\\n\\r\\n### Static VPN Has Higher Priority Than DX\\r\\n\\r\\n- Static VPN routes have a **higher routing priority** at the TGW than Direct Connect routes\\r\\n- Always refer to the TGW Route evaluation order when determining which attachment path will win for a given prefix\\r\\n- This can cause unexpected behavior if a customer has both a static VPN and DX advertising the same prefix \u2014 the static VPN will be preferred\\r\\n\\r\\n### Path Selection Wording: ECMP Is an Outcome, Not a Step\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Longest prefix match comes first.** It is a route lookup, not a BGP attribute.\\r\\n- For routes with the same prefix, the BGP attributes are compared in order and **selection stops at the first attribute that differs**. For routes of the same attachment type at the TGW, the documented tiebreakers are shorter AS_PATH, then lower MED, then eBGP over iBGP ([route evaluation order](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html)).\\r\\n- If every compared attribute is equal and the ECMP conditions below are met, the **result** is ECMP. ECMP is never an attribute or a step in the order.\\r\\n- **Routes from DXGW attachments are a special case:** **[Field knowledge, SME-confirmed]** the BGP attributes (LP communities, AS_PATH prepends, MED) are set at the **VIF level**, on the advertisements the on-prem router sends over each VIF, and are evaluated by the DXGW / Direct Connect side. They do not pass to the TGW, and the TGW does not compare them. Direct Connect compares the VIF advertisements across the DXGWs and the TGW installs the result (see \"ECMP Across Multiple DXGW Attachments\" below).\\r\\n\\r\\n## ECMP Behavior\\r\\n\\r\\n### How the TGW Sees a Direct Connect Gateway (Two-Lookup Model)\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery construct that owns a route table does its own route lookup. The DXGW is not a forwarding hop: AWS describes it as \"a distributed set of BGP route reflectors\" that \"operates outside the data traffic path\" ([Direct Connect gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-gateways-intro.html)).\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Lookup 1, at the DXGW (control plane):** the DXGW receives on-prem prefixes over its transit VIFs, evaluates the BGP attributes on each VIF\\'s advertisements (set by the on-prem router per VIF) using the DX rules (longest prefix match, then local preference \u2192 AS_PATH length \u2192 MED), and reflects the result to the TGW. If the attributes are equal across VIFs, the result of this selection is ECMP across those VIFs.\\r\\n- **Lookup 2, at the TGW route table:** for on-prem prefixes the TGW sees the DXGW attachment as (usually) a single next hop. The TGW route table shows **one entry per prefix per DXGW attachment** (when two DXGW attachments qualify for ECMP, both appear as next hops for the prefix; see below).\\r\\n- **Data path:** traffic forwarded by the TGW goes straight to the VIF(s) the DXGW selected. Packets do not go through a second lookup at the DXGW.\\r\\n\\r\\nConsequences:\\r\\n- One TGW route-table entry per DXGW attachment does **not** mean one active VIF. VIF load sharing happens inside the DXGW\\'s own selection. The TGW docs state that \"A single Direct Connect gateway supports ECMP across multiple transit virtual interfaces,\" and AWS recommends using a single Direct Connect gateway rather than multiple gateways to take advantage of ECMP ([route evaluation order](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html)).\\r\\n- You do not need multiple DXGWs to get multiple active DX paths. Use **one DXGW with multiple transit VIFs** for ECMP.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Supported ECMP Scenarios\\r\\n\\r\\n- **VPN attachments**: TGW supports ECMP across VPN attachments when \"VPN ECMP support\" is enabled on the TGW. To use ECMP the VPN connection must use **dynamic (BGP) routing**; ECMP is not supported on static VPN connections ([VPN quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-limits.html), [TGW quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/transit-gateway-quotas.html)).\\r\\n- **Multiple transit VIFs on one DXGW (recommended)**: ECMP is the result of the DXGW\\'s own selection when the BGP attributes on the VIF advertisements are equal. The TGW still shows one entry for that DXGW attachment.\\r\\n- **Multiple DXGW attachments**: see the next section.\\r\\n- **Multiple TGW Connect attachments**: TGW will ECMP across matching prefixes\\r\\n\\r\\n### ECMP Across Multiple DXGW Attachments\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Documented condition:** the prefix, prefix length and AS_PATH must be **exactly the same**. BGP Multipath AS-Path Relax is not supported, so there is no ECMP across different ASNs ([route evaluation order](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html)).\\r\\n- **[Field knowledge, lab-validated]** The routes also need **equal MED** and AS_PATHs that contain **exactly the same ASNs** (equal length alone is not enough).\\r\\n- **[Field knowledge, SME-confirmed]** The DXGWs\\' **Amazon-side ASNs must match** (see \"DXGW Amazon-Side ASNs Must Match for ECMP\" below).\\r\\n- **TGW-specific:** this Direct Connect-side cross-DXGW decision applies to a TGW. Cloud WAN works differently: the CNE learns the route from each DXGW attachment and runs its own route evaluation, steered by Cloud WAN routing policies (see \"Multiple DXGWs on Cloud WAN\" in cloudwan-dx-routing-patterns.md).\\r\\n- **[Field knowledge, SME-confirmed] Where the decision is made:** the ECMP decision is made on the **Direct Connect side**, not by the TGW comparing attributes. The BGP attributes are VIF-level (set on the on-prem router\\'s advertisements over each VIF) and do not pass to the TGW. Direct Connect compares the VIF BGP advertisements across the DXGWs using **all** the BGP attributes, in this order:\\r\\n  1. Longest prefix match (a route lookup, not a BGP attribute)\\r\\n  2. Local preference \u2014 LP communities (`7224:7300/7200/7100`) and the local-Region default\\r\\n  3. AS_PATH length\\r\\n  4. MED\\r\\n\\r\\n  Selection stops at the first attribute that differs.\\r\\n  - If all of them match, Direct Connect sends all of those DXGW attachments to the TGW and the TGW installs them as **ECMP next hops**. The TGW route table lists **every** qualifying DXGW attachment for the prefix, the same way it lists multiple VPN connections for VPN ECMP.\\r\\n  - If they do not match, only a **single** DXGW attachment (the winner) is installed for the prefix.\\r\\n- **In-account check:** `aws ec2 search-transit-gateway-routes` for the prefix. **Two (or more) DXGW attachments listed = ECMP. One attachment listed = a single path.**\\r\\n\\r\\n### NOT Supported\\r\\n\\r\\n- **ECMP across different attachment types** \u2014 TGW does NOT ECMP between, for example, a DX-GW attachment and a VPN attachment for the same prefix. Instead, the Route evaluation order determines the winner.\\r\\n- **Multipath AS-Path Relax** \u2014 ECMP for paths with different AS_PATHs (including different ASNs) is NOT supported.\\r\\n\\r\\n### When Routes From Multiple DXGW Attachments Do Not Qualify for ECMP\\r\\n\\r\\n- If one route wins on an attribute (local preference, AS_PATH length, MED), only that DXGW attachment is installed.\\r\\n- If no attribute separates them but they still do not qualify for ECMP (for example, equal AS_PATH length but different ASNs), only one attachment is installed in the TGW route table, and you can\\'t control which one.\\r\\n  - Documented: for routes with the same CIDR, attachment type and BGP attributes, AWS \"can\\'t guarantee a consistent route prioritization order\" ([route evaluation order](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html)). The winner can differ between prefixes and can change over time, for example after a route is withdrawn and re-advertised.\\r\\n  - **[Field knowledge]** The pick is made from a hash of the prefix metadata, so in practice a given prefix often lands on the same attachment. That is an observation, not a guarantee.\\r\\n  - Do not design around which attachment wins an exact tie. Separate the routes with an attribute (local preference, AS_PATH length or MED), or make them qualify for ECMP.\\r\\n\\r\\n### DXGW Amazon-Side ASNs Must Match for ECMP\\r\\n\\r\\n**[Field knowledge, SME-confirmed]** For TGW ECMP across multiple DXGW attachments, the DXGWs\\' **Amazon-side ASNs must match**. The AS_PATH compared across DXGWs must be exactly the same, and AS-Path Relax is not supported, so DXGWs with different Amazon-side ASNs do not qualify for ECMP; a single attachment is installed instead. Examples:\\r\\n   - **Attachment isolation (on-prem firewall hairpin):** separate allowed-prefix lists and separate TGW route-table associations per DXGW, so traffic between VPCs is sent through an on-prem firewall and back ([re:Post: route VPC traffic through an on-prem firewall over a transit VIF](https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/route-vpc-traffic-with-dc-transit-vif)).\\r\\n   - **VPC isolation:** the DXGW docs list provisioning a separate DXGW per VPC as a mitigation to block VPC-to-VPC communication through a shared DXGW ([Direct Connect gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-gateways-intro.html); see \"VPC-to-VPC Traffic via a DXGW\" in dx-routing-patterns.md).\\r\\n2. **Architectures that need multiple primary paths**, for example Asia needs a different primary DX location than North America. Use this knowledge when advising on active/active, active/passive, and failover architectures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reference Documentation\\r\\n\\r\\n- [AWS Site-to-Site VPN routing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPNRoutingTypes.html)\\r\\n- [Direct Connect routing policies and BGP communities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html)\\r\\n- [DX Resiliency Recommendations](https://aws.amazon.com/directconnect/resiliency-recommendation/)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Assumptions\\r\\n\\r\\n- Customer\\'s network does not overlap with VPC CIDR\\r\\n- Customer Gateway (CGW) device is configured to handle asymmetric routing\\r\\n- Static VPN tunnels are Route-Based only (not Policy-Based)\\r\\n- Customer advertises the same on-prem routes through all redundant connections (DX and VPN)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Key Behavior: VGW Does NOT ECMP Across VPN Connections\\r\\n\\r\\nA VGW does **not** use Equal-Cost Multi-Path routing (ECMP) across VPN tunnels or VPN connections. Customer can influence by:\\r\\n  - Advertising **lower AS-path** to VGW over the desired tunnel\\r\\n  - Advertising **lower MED** to VGW over the desired tunnel\\r\\n\\r\\n### DX Connection with Backup VPN\\r\\n\\r\\n- DX is **always preferred over VPN** for return traffic to the same on-prem subnet\\r\\n- Customer must ensure on-prem traffic is sent over DX when both are UP\\r\\n- Attempting to prefer VPN over DX will cause asymmetric routing (VGW always returns via DX)\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2 DX Connections (Same VGW)\\r\\n\\r\\n- 2 private VIFs to the same VGW over 2 DX connections\\r\\n- **Active/Active:** Equal LP + AS-path on CGW \u2192 return traffic is flow-hashed across both DX connections\\r\\n- **Active/Passive:** Unequal LP + AS-path \u2192 customer-to-VPC uses the higher LP set on the customer router; VPC-to-customer uses the higher DX local-preference community, then the lower AS-path (see below)\\r\\n- **DX local-preference communities are honored on private VIFs attached directly to a VGW** (documented for private and transit VIFs in [Private virtual interface and transit virtual interface routing policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html#private-routing-policies)): tagging `7224:7300` (high), `7224:7200` (medium) or `7224:7100` (low) on the advertisements sent over each VIF steers VPC-to-customer (AWS \u2192 on-prem) traffic. VPC \u2192 Customer always traverses single tunnel (Preferred Tunnel)\\r\\n- If customer sends traffic on CGW 2, return may come back on CGW 1 \u2192 **asymmetric routing**\\r\\n- Only works if CGW devices have synchronization (ECMP) and accept asymmetric traffic\\r\\n\\r\\n### \u274c 2 BGP VPN Connections with Same LP and AS-Path from 2 CGW Devices\\r\\n\\r\\n- Same problem as static: VPC routing\\r\\n\\r\\n### \u274c DX + VPN \u2014 Attempting to Prefer VPN Over DX\\r\\n\\r\\n- If customer tries to prefer VPN over DX, return traffic (VPC \u2192 on-prem) STILL goes over DX\\r\\n- VGW **The limit you're hitting:** the Site-to-Site VPN connection on a TGW can advertise at most **5,000 routes** to the customer gateway device — and that quota is **not adjustable**. The routes it advertises come from the **TGW route table associated with that VPN attachment**.

**What happens when you're over the cap:** TGW picks what to advertise in this order — static routes before propagated routes, and within the same type, least-specific first. That's the mechanism you want to exploit: a static summary survives the cap while the individual propagated routes it covers get trimmed. (This selection order isn't on the public TGW route-evaluation page — it's field-validated — so confirm it in your account before relying on it.)

**The safe way to summarize — don't touch propagation:**
1. **Leave VPC propagation enabled.** Those individual VPC CIDRs (/16s, /24s) must stay in the TGW route table — they're what the TGW uses for the *return* path (VPN → individual VPCs) via longest-prefix-match in the data plane. Removing propagation to "make room" is what breaks the return path.
2. **Add a static summary route** (e.g., `10.0.0.0/14` covering a set of /16 VPC CIDRs) in the same TGW route table, pointed at a persistent attachment.
3. Under the advertisement cap, the static summary gets advertised preferentially (static-before-propagated, least-specific-first), consuming just **1 slot** in the 5,000-route VPN budget instead of hundreds.
4. Any propagated specifics that get cut off from the advertisement list are still covered reachability-wise by the summary.
5. **Return traffic is unaffected** — the TGW still does longest-prefix-match internally, so the more-specific propagated /16s win over the /14 summary for actual forwarding, regardless of what got advertised out to on-prem.

**One thing to get right:** point the static summary at a persistent attachment — a shared-services/firewall VPC, or a dedicated "dummy" VPC built just to anchor the route (propagation disabled on it, tagged as non-deletable). If the attachment it points to is ever deleted, the summary blackholes, and blackholed routes aren't advertised — which would silently drop the aggregated prefixes.

**Also note:** all routes across all TGW route tables share a separate, TGW-wide quota of 10,000 total combined routes (adjustable via SA/TAM) — summarization doesn't affect that count since you're still holding both the static summary and the propagated specifics.

If summarization still doesn't fit (e.g., non-contiguous CIDRs that can't aggregate), the alternatives are **TGW Connect** (GRE+BGP, 5,000-route cap per peer, scales horizontally with multiple peers) or splitting across **multiple VPN connections** with route tables segmented so each stays under 5,000.

**Validate in-account (read-only):**
```
aws ec2 search-transit-gateway-routes --transit-gateway-route-table-id <rtb-id> --filters Name=type,Values=static
aws ec2 get-transit-gateway-route-table-associations --transit-gateway-route-table-id <rtb-id>
aws ec2 search-transit-gateway-routes --transit-gateway-route-table-id <rtb-id> --filters Name=type,Values=propagated
```
